steps.say: Tamponade announces itself with three bedside signs, not with machines, demanding immediate action. Systemic hypotension pairs with muffled or distant heart sounds and a distended jugular venous pulse. When all three gather in a breathless child, the pericardium is strangling the heart.
steps.tx: The **Beck triad** of **cardiac tamponade** comprises systemic **hypotension**, muffled or **distant heart sounds**, and elevated **jugular venous distension**. Rising intrapericardial pressure chokes diastolic filling, so stroke volume falls while venous pressure climbs. The triad at the bedside outruns any single pressure number in speed.

vis.alt: Diagram showing heart compressed by fluid, illustrating Beck's triad, pulsus paradoxus, and echocardiographic right atrial collapse, with pericardiocentesis.
vis.caption: Cardiac tamponade: life-threatening compression of the heart by pericardial fluid. Image: www.scientificanimations.com, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

steps.say: The blood pressure itself gives the next clue. In tamponade the systolic pressure falls by more than 10 millimetres of mercury with each normal inspiration, an exaggeration called pulsus paradoxus. Inspiration fills the right heart at the expense of the left, and the pulse fades on cue.
steps.tx: **Pulsus paradoxus** is an exaggerated **inspiratory decrease in systolic arterial pressure** exceeding **10 mmHg** during normal breathing. Inspiratory right heart filling bows the septum leftwards and curtails left ventricular output. The **palpable pulse weakens with inspiration** and returns with expiration, a sign measured with a slow cuff deflation.

nodes.label: Inspiration fills the right heart chambers
Septum bows left and LV output dips

steps.say: Echocardiography confirms what the hands suspect. Early diastolic collapse of the right ventricle and late diastolic collapse of the right atrium mark chambers buckling under fluid pressure. Reciprocal respiratory swings in valve inflow above 25 to 40 percent, sealing the diagnosis.
steps.tx: Key **echocardiographic tamponade signs** are **early diastolic collapse of the right ventricle**, **late diastolic collapse of the right atrium**, and **reciprocal respiratory inflow variations above 25-40%** across valves. Low pressure right chambers buckle first because they cannot resist the surrounding fluid. A large **circumferential effusion** with these signs needs drainage, not observation.

vis.alt: Apical echo shows a large circumferential pericardial effusion with early diastolic right ventricular collapse and right atrial inversion.
vis.caption: Tamponade echo with effusion and right heart collapse. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.say: The ECG and the chest film add their own fingerprints, pointing to the pericardium. Beat to beat alternation of QRS height and axis, called electrical alternans, reflects the heart swinging within a large effusion. A symmetric globular water bottle silhouette needs at least 200 to 250 millilitres of fluid in an older child.
steps.tx: **Electrical alternans** is beat to beat alternation of **QRS complex amplitude and axis**, reflecting swinging of the heart within a large effusion. The **water bottle heart** is a symmetric globular silhouette requiring at least **200-250 mL** of pericardial fluid in older children. Low voltage complexes with a huge cardiac shadow point straight at the pericardium.

points: Beat to beat QRS amplitude alternation
Axis swings with the swinging heart

steps.say: When tamponade physiology is present, the needle cannot wait for morning. Pericardiocentesis through the subxiphoid route under continuous echocardiographic and ECG monitoring drains the compressing fluid and restores filling within minutes. The ECG watch guards against touching the epicardium with the needle tip.
steps.tx: **Emergency pericardiocentesis** via the **subxiphoid approach** under continuous **echocardiographic and ECG monitoring** is life saving in tamponade. Fluid removal drops intrapericardial pressure and lets the chambers fill again. ST elevation on the needle ECG warns of epicardial contact, and a pigtail catheter stays when reaccumulation threatens.

steps.say: Pericarditis without tamponade tells its story on the ECG first. Stage 1 shows diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression across limb and precordial leads, while aVR and V1 show the mirror image of PR elevation. The changes span territories no single coronary could explain.
steps.tx: The **acute pericarditis ECG stages** begin with stage 1: diffuse **concave ST elevation** with **PR depression** across limb and precordial leads, except **aVR and V1 which show PR elevation**. Widespread concave elevation without reciprocal depression separates pericarditis from infarction. The PR segment shifts first and normalises first, so early tracings carry the most information.

vis.alt: Medical illustration of acute pericarditis showing fibrinous exudate between the parietal and visceral pericardium generating an auscultatory friction rub, accompanied by an ECG showing diffuse concave ST elevation and P
vis.caption: Fibrinous pericarditis with friction rub and diffuse ST elevation with PR depression. Tamponade physiology needs urgent drainage. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Most idiopathic and viral cases settle with pills, not procedures, healing over weeks. First line treatment pairs NSAIDs such as ibuprofen with weight adjusted colchicine for 3 months to prevent recurrences. Rest and avoidance of competitive sport continue until symptoms, ECG, and inflammatory markers normalise.
steps.tx: **Medical therapy for acute pericarditis** is first line for **idiopathic or viral pericarditis**: **NSAIDs (ibuprofen)** with weight adjusted **colchicine for 3 months** to prevent recurrences. Colchicine halves relapse compared with NSAIDs alone. Corticosteroids are reserved for contraindications, systemic disease, or refractory cases because they invite rebound on withdrawal.

steps.say: Not every effusion behaves benignly, so follow-up has a plan. Purulent, tuberculous, and recurrent large effusions need cause directed therapy and often a surgical window. Any drift toward constriction with breathlessness and liver congestion earns pericardiectomy review before the shell starts hardening.
steps.tx: Purulent and **tuberculous effusions** need prolonged cause directed therapy plus drainage, while recurrent large idiopathic effusions earn a **perisurgical window** discussion. Emerging **constriction** with exercise intolerance, ascites, and a thickened pericardium shifts management toward **pericardiectomy**. Serial echo and inflammatory markers decide whether the trajectory bends toward healing or surgery.
